entry: Problem of determining whether a Boolean formula can be made true. It asks whether some assignment of TRUE or FALSE to the formula's variables makes the formula evaluate to TRUE. SAT was the first problem proven to be NP-complete. No known algorithm solves every instance in polynomial time, and resolving whether one exists would settle the [[P versus NP problem]]. Heuristic solvers nonetheless handle instances with tens of thousands of variables, enough for many practical uses in [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]], [[Circuit design|circuit design]] and automatic theorem proving.

Thrown tool with airfoil-shaped sections, designed to spin in flight. Returning boomerangs are built to come back to the thrower, a meaning preserved in official competitions. Non-returning throwing sticks were also used for hunting. The word comes from an [[Aboriginal Australians|Aboriginal Australian]] language of the Sydney region. Historically, boomerangs served as hunting weapons, percussive musical instruments, [[Club (weapon)|battle clubs]], fire-starters and toys. The oldest surviving Aboriginal boomerang, held by the South Australian Museum, was found in a peat bog in South Australia and dated to 10,000 BC. A mammoth-tusk example from Obłazowa Cave in Poland is believed to be about 40,000 years old. Similar throwing sticks have been found in [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]] and North America.

Type of footwear covering the foot and ankle, and often part of the lower leg. Most boots have a heel clearly distinct from the sole and are traditionally made of leather or rubber. They protect the foot from water, mud, cold, insects and sharp hazards, and they provide ankle support for [[Hiking|hiking]]. Some jurisdictions require steel-toed boots for construction workers. Around 1000 BC, separate leggings, soles and uppers were joined into single units. [[Nomad|Nomads]] in eastern Asia wore soft leather ankle boots, and the [[Inuit]] and Aleut peoples of Alaska developed winter boots of caribou skin or sealskin. Thigh-high boots worn by Hessian soldiers in the [[American Revolutionary War]] influenced the heeled cowboy boots of the American West. High-top athletic [[Shoe|shoes]] are generally not considered boots because they lack a distinct heel.

Volcanic island in the Society Islands of [[French Polynesia]]. Surrounded by a lagoon and barrier reef, the main island has a land area of 30.55 sq km. Its highest point, Mount Otemanu, rises 727 m (2,385 ft) from the remnants of an extinct volcano. Tahitian and French are the main languages, and the island is known for luxury resorts. [[James Cook]] sighted it in 1769. France annexed the island as a colony in 1888. During [[World War II]], the United States built a supply base there.

Hydrated sodium borate, a [[Salt (chemistry)|salt]] of [[Boric acid|boric acid]]. Borax is a white crystalline solid, with the formula Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O, that dissolves in water to form a basic solution. The naturally occurring mineral, called tincal, was historically mined from dry lake beds in Asia and traded along the [[Silk Road]]. In the late 19th century the Pacific Coast Borax Company popularized it in the United States under the 20 Mule Team Borax trademark. It is used as a [[Pesticide|pesticide]], metal soldering flux and component of [[Glass|glass]] and pottery glazes.

Port city on the Garonne River, capital of Nouvelle-Aquitaine (pop., 2023: 267,991). It is the prefecture of the Gironde department in southwestern France. The Bordeaux metropolitan area had 1,426,278 residents in 2023. The city is a center of wine: vineyards and châteaux stand on the hillsides of the Gironde, and it hosts Vinexpo, the world's main wine fair. The aeronautics and space industry is based there, with companies including Dassault Aviation, ArianeGroup, Safran and Thales. The city has more than 362 historic monuments, after [[Paris]] the most in France. Its Port of the Moon was inscribed on the [[UNESCO]] World Heritage List in 2007. The Romans ruled Bordeaux from about 60 BC, when it became a commercial center for [[Tin|tin]] and [[Lead|lead]]. The [[Vandals]] sacked it in 276 AD, and the [[Visigoths]] and [[Franks]] later attacked it.

Geographic boundary of a [[Sovereign state|sovereign state]] or other political entity. Borders may follow oceans or terrain, or be set through warfare, [[Colonization|colonization]] or agreement. Some borders, such as internal administrative lines and those within the [[Schengen Area]], are open and unguarded. External borders are usually controlled and may be crossed legally only at checkpoints, which include airports and seaports. Under international law, each country generally sets the conditions for crossing its borders. The area around a border is called the frontier. Enforcement measures such as barriers and surveillance are debated: proponents see them as essential to sovereignty, while critics argue they obstruct global equity.

Personality disorder marked by unstable relationships, self-image and emotions. Symptoms include an extreme fear of abandonment, intense emotional outbursts, impulsive or self-harming behavior, and a pervasive sense of emptiness. The disorder usually emerges in early adulthood and often occurs alongside [[Substance use disorder|substance use disorders]], [[Mood disorder|depressive disorders]] and eating disorders. Studies estimate that up to 10 percent of people with the disorder die by [[Suicide|suicide]], a rate about 730 times greater than that of the general population in the United States. The current hypothesis holds that genetic factors interact with adverse childhood experiences. [[Psychotherapy|Psychotherapy]], especially dialectical behavior therapy and schema therapy, is the most effective treatment. [[Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor|SSRI]] antidepressants and atypical antipsychotics may ease symptoms but cannot cure the disorder. In the U.S., around 1% of the population is diagnosed with it.

[[Emotion]] of uninterest in one's surroundings. Boredom is often caused by a lack of distractions or occupations, and it is distinct from [[Depression (mood)|depression]] and apathy. It may damage mental health, but it can also stimulate [[Creativity|creativity]]. Psychologists describe it as a state of lacking engagement, and boredom proneness is clearly associated with [[Attention|attention]] lapses. Robert Plutchik characterized boredom as a mild form of disgust. A popular misconception credits [[Charles Dickens]] with coining the word in *Bleak House* (1853), but it has been attested since at least 1829. The German word *Langeweile* combines the words for long and while.

Class of nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines for the Russian Navy. Built by Sevmash in Severodvinsk, the class is replacing the Soviet-era Delta III and Delta IV classes. At 24,000 tons submerged and with 107 crew, Borei-class boats are much smaller than the 48,000-ton Typhoon class. The lead vessel, Yury Dolgorukiy, was rolled out in 2007 and began sea trials in the [[White Sea]] in 2009.

Weak acid of [[Boron|boron]], with formula B(OH)₃. It is usually encountered as colorless crystals or a white powder that dissolves in water to form a mildly acidic solution, and it occurs in nature as the mineral sassolite. Boric acid is used as an antiseptic, insecticide, flame retardant and neutron absorber, and as a precursor to other boron compounds. Wilhelm Homberg first prepared it from [[Borax|borax]] by the action of mineral acids. It can react with alcohols to form borate esters. When heated, it loses water in stages, first forming metaboric acid above about 140 °C.

German former professional [[Tennis|tennis]] player and coach. He won six [[Grand Slam (tennis)|Grand Slam]] singles titles, including three at Wimbledon, and was ranked world No. 1 by the ATP. At 17 he became the youngest-ever men's singles champion at Wimbledon. He coached [[Novak Djokovic]] from 2013 to 2016. In 2002 a [[Munich]] court gave him a suspended prison sentence for tax evasion. In 2022 UK courts sentenced him to two and a half years for hiding assets from creditors; he was released after eight months.

Knyaz of the [[First Bulgarian Empire]] (r. 852–889). After baptism he took the Christian name Michael. The [[Christianity|Christianization]] of Bulgaria in 864 abolished paganism. He exploited the rivalry between the Patriarchate of [[Constantinople]] and the Papacy to secure an autocephalous Bulgarian Church. In 885 he gave refuge to the disciples of [[Cyril and Methodius]] after they were banished from [[Great Moravia]]. This saved the Glagolitic script and later promoted the [[Cyrillic script|Cyrillic]] script and Slavic literature. He abdicated in 889. His eldest son tried to restore paganism, but Boris deposed him, and the subsequent Council of Preslav replaced Byzantine clergy with native Bulgarians. The Orthodox Church venerates him as a saint.

British politician and writer, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom (2019–22). He was Mayor of London from 2008 to 2016 and a prominent campaigner in the 2016 [[Brexit]] referendum. The UK left the EU in January 2020 under his premiership, and his government oversaw a fast [[COVID-19]] vaccination programme. He resigned in 2022 after mass ministerial resignations. In 2023 a parliamentary committee unanimously found that he had lied to the House of Commons. Supporters credit him with delivering Brexit; critics accuse him of dishonesty, elitism and cronyism.

English actor known for horror roles. Born William Henry Pratt, he is best known for playing the monster in *Frankenstein* (1931), a role he reprised in *Bride of Frankenstein* (1935) and *Son of Frankenstein* (1939). He appeared in 174 films and voiced the Grinch in the animated special *How the Grinch Stole Christmas!* (1966), which won him a Grammy Award. He received two stars on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 1960.

Russian and Soviet poet, novelist and translator. Born in Moscow into a [[Jews|Jewish]] family, he was the son of the painter Leonid Pasternak. His first poetry collection, *My Sister, Life*, was published in Berlin in 1922. His translations of Goethe, Schiller, Calderón and Shakespeare remain popular in Russian theatre scholarship. The novel *Doctor Zhivago* (1957) is set between the [[Russian Revolution of 1905]] and World War II. Rejected for publication in the [[Soviet Union]], its manuscript was first published in Italy in 1957. Pasternak was awarded the 1958 [[Nobel Prize|Nobel Prize]] in Literature, but the [[Communist Party of the Soviet Union|Communist Party]] forced him to decline it. His son accepted the prize on his behalf in 1989.

Soviet and Russian politician, president of Russia (1991–99). He was the first person to resign from the Politburo, in 1987. Elected to lead the Russian republic's Supreme Soviet in 1990, he became president in 1991, the first popularly elected head of state in Russian history. He was instrumental in the [[Dissolution of the Soviet Union|dissolution of the Soviet Union]] in December 1991. His economic shock therapy liberalized prices and privatized state assets, followed by inflation and the rise of oligarchs. In 1993 he ordered the parliament dissolved, and loyal troops stormed the parliament building. Secessionist conflict in the Caucasus led to the [[First Chechen War]] and the Second Chechen War, between 1994 and 1999. He resigned at the end of 1999 and was succeeded by his chosen successor, [[Vladimir Putin]]. Supporters credit him with dismantling the Soviet Union and introducing new freedoms; critics accuse him of economic mismanagement, corruption and abuse of presidential power.

Third-largest island in the world, in Maritime Southeast Asia. It covers 748,168 sq km, and its population was 23,053,723 in 2020. The [[Equator]] crosses it roughly in half. The island is divided among [[Indonesia]], which holds about 73% as the provinces of Kalimantan; [[Malaysia]], with about 26% as the states of Sabah and Sarawak; and [[Brunei]], which occupies a small area. Its many Indigenous communities are often grouped under the broad term Dayak. The Sultanate of Brunei held influence over much of the coast in the 15th century. Parts of the island were colonized by Britain, the Netherlands and Japan. Logging and agricultural conversion have cut into forests that include some of the oldest tropical [[Rainforest|rainforests]] in the world. It is the site of Indonesia's planned capital, Nusantara.

9th-century [[Mahayana]] Buddhist temple in Central Java, Indonesia. Built under the Sailendra dynasty, it is a stack of nine platforms, six square and three circular, topped by a central dome. It is decorated with 2,672 relief panels and originally held 504 Buddha statues, 72 of them seated in perforated stupas around the dome. Abandoned after the decline of Hindu kingdoms in Java and the conversion to Islam, it was brought to worldwide attention in 1814 by Thomas Stamford Raffles. A restoration completed in 1983 by the Indonesian government and [[UNESCO]] preserved it, and it is a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]]. It remains a major site of [[Pilgrimage|pilgrimage]].

Chemical element (symbol B, atomic number 5). The lightest member of the boron group, it is a brittle, lustrous [[Metalloid|metalloid]] in crystalline form and forms covalent bonds in compounds such as [[Boric acid|boric acid]] and the ultra-hard boron carbide and boron nitride. It makes up about 0.001 percent of Earth's crust and occurs in nature only in compounds, mainly borate minerals such as [[Borax|borax]]. The largest known deposits are in [[Turkey]], the largest producer of boron minerals. About half of world production is used as an additive in fiberglass. Borosilicate glass and sodium perborate bleach are other major uses. Boron is also a [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]] dopant and an essential plant nutrient. [[Humphry Davy]] isolated it in 1808, and [[Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac]] and Louis Jacques Thénard also produced it.

Sour soup made with meat stock and vegetables, common in [[Eastern Europe]] and [[Central Europe]]. The Ukrainian version is colored red by [[Beetroot|beetroot]] and typically includes cabbage, carrots, onions, potatoes and tomatoes. The English name derives through [[Yiddish]] from a Slavic word for hogweed, the plant used in the ancient soup. Jews and Mennonites brought borscht to [[North America]]. In 2022 [[UNESCO]] inscribed the "Culture of Ukrainian borscht cooking" on its list of intangible cultural heritage needing urgent safeguarding, noting that other countries also practice borscht cooking.

Nine-level numeric scale for the brightness of the night sky. Amateur astronomer John E. Bortle devised it and published it in February 2001 in *Sky & Telescope*. It ranges from Class 1, the darkest skies, where the [[Milky Way]] is prominent, to Class 9, inner-city skies. Its classes correspond closely to naked-eye limiting magnitude and sky quality meter readings. Amateur and professional astronomers widely use it. A 2014 study suggested that it may overestimate the visibility of dim objects.

State of matter formed by cooling a dilute gas of [[Boson|bosons]] to temperatures close to [[Absolute zero|absolute zero]]. Most bosons then occupy the lowest quantum state, so quantum effects such as wave interference become visible on a macroscopic scale. [[Albert Einstein]] predicted the condensate in 1924–25, building on a paper by [[Satyendra Nath Bose]] on quantum statistics. On June 5, 1995, Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman of the University of Colorado Boulder produced the first gaseous condensate, using rubidium atoms cooled to 170 nanokelvins. Later that year Wolfgang Ketterle at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] produced one with sodium atoms. Cornell, Wieman and Ketterle shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physics. In 1938 Fritz London proposed the condensate as a mechanism for [[Superfluidity|superfluidity]] in helium-4.

[[Civil war|Civil war]] in Japan (1868–69) between the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] and an imperial coalition. Samurai from the Chōshū, Satsuma and Tosa domains secured the Imperial Court and [[Emperor Meiji]]. After the shogun Tokugawa Yoshinobu handed over power, his loyalists fought on, and the last of them were defeated at Hakodate on [[Hokkaido]] in 1869. About 69,000 men were mobilized, and about 8,200 were killed. The victors adopted modernization, and many former shogunate leaders were later given government posts.

Country on the Balkan Peninsula in southeastern Europe. It borders [[Serbia]], [[Montenegro]] and [[Croatia]], with a 20 km coast on the Adriatic Sea. The country is largely mountainous, and [[Sarajevo]] is the capital and largest city. The [[Ottoman Empire]] annexed the region in 1463 and introduced Islam. After Austro-Hungarian rule and a period in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, it declared independence in 1992. The [[Bosnian War]] lasted until late 1995 and ended with the Dayton Agreement. Bosniaks make up half of the population of around 3.4 million, followed by Serbs and Croats. The country has two highly autonomous entities, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and [[Republika Srpska]], plus the Brčko District. It has been an [[European Union|EU]] candidate since 2022.
